t: Which cause of vaginitis is it?
key: Sort by pH first: above 4.5 means bacterial vaginosis or trichomoniasis, and a normal pH means candidiasis. Then let the slide decide: clue cells, motile trichomonads, or pseudohyphae.
items: Epithelial cells coated with Gardnerella and anaerobes are the microscopic hallmark of vaginosis.
Anaerobes make amines that turn volatile and fishy when potassium hydroxide is added.
Vaginosis is a flora shift without inflammation, so the discharge is thin and coats the walls.
Few white cells despite heavy discharge
Vaginosis is not an inflammatory infection, so neutrophils stay scarce on the slide.
Losing lactic acid producers lets Gardnerella and anaerobes take over and raise the pH.
Punctate cervical hemorrhages from the protozoan's inflammation are a classic trichomoniasis sign.
Pear-shaped trichomonads swim on a saline wet mount when the slide is read promptly.
The profuse, bubbly discharge reflects active inflammation by the protozoan.
Trichomoniasis is sexually transmitted, so untreated partners cause reinfection.
NAAT more sensitive than wet mount
The wet mount misses up to half of infections, so amplification testing is preferred.
A KOH prep dissolves squamous cells and leaves the fungal forms of Candida in view.
Candida tolerates acid and can overgrow while lactobacilli keep the pH at 4.5 or below.
The cottage cheese discharge with intense itching is typical of yeast infection.
Antibiotics kill the lactobacilli that normally restrain Candida overgrowth.
Fluconazole blocks fungal ergosterol synthesis and cures most uncomplicated episodes.
